title: Duplicated western blot bands
scenario: Postdoctoral researcher Ngozi Adeyemi in a Toronto cancer lab notices that two lanes in a figure from her supervisor's famous paper look like the same band, flipped and relabelled. The paper underpins the lab's current grant and her own project. The supervisor, Professor Reinhardt, wrote her recommendation letter and controls her visa sponsorship. She has no proof of intent, only the images. Ngozi must decide what to do with her suspicion.
options: Quietly ask Reinhardt for the raw blots, giving him a chance to explain or correct before anything formal happens.
Report the image to the university's research integrity office confidentially, accepting the personal risk to her visa and career.
Say nothing for now and verify the key result in her own experiments first, delaying any action until she has evidence.

title: Rounding a p-value just under the line
scenario: Doctoral student Kwame Boateng in Accra has spent three years on a study of a low-cost maternal health intervention. His final analysis gives p = 0.054. His advisor suggests dropping two outlier clinics, justified post hoc as 'data entry problems,' which pushes the result under 0.05 and makes the paper publishable in a respected journal. The clinics did have some messy records. Kwame's funding ends in two months. He must decide how to proceed.
options: Drop the clinics as suggested, since the records were messy and the advisor has more experience judging data quality.
Report the result as it stands at p = 0.054, accepting a harder path to publication and an unhappy advisor.
Report both analyses openly, with and without the clinics, and let readers judge, risking rejection and conflict.

title: A fabricated site in a multi-centre trial
scenario: Data monitor Svetlana Petrova at a contract research firm in Sofia is reviewing a pharmaceutical trial. One site in another country reports dozens of patients with strikingly similar blood pressure readings, and signature dates fall on weekends when the clinic is closed. If the site is excluded, the drug's benefit may vanish and a potentially useful medicine could be shelved. The sponsor is pressing for on-time database lock. Svetlana must decide how to flag it.
options: Escalate immediately to the sponsor's quality team and regulators, seeking a formal audit even if it delays the trial.
Quietly request source documents from the site first, in case there is an innocent explanation, before escalating.
Report the anomaly in the standard monitoring log and leave the decision about exclusion to the sponsor's statisticians.

title: Reanalysing a retired colleague's dataset
scenario: Environmental statistician Dr. Matteo Ricci in Bologna inherits the dataset of a revered, recently deceased professor whose well-cited paper links a pesticide to soil microbe decline. While cleaning, he finds that about fifteen percent of samples were excluded without explanation, and that including them weakens the effect substantially. The professor's family and institute are planning a memorial volume. Regulation discussions cite the paper. Matteo must choose what to do.
options: Publish a reanalysis with the excluded samples and note the discrepancy, even though the professor cannot respond.
Contact the journal privately with a request for a correction and let editors handle communication with the family.
Delay any action until he can find the professor's notes explaining the exclusions, risking that none exist.
tension: respect for the dead vs. scientific correction

title: Reproducing a result that will not reproduce
scenario: Lab manager Priya Venkataraman in Bengaluru has tried for eight months to replicate a published synthesis method from a prominent chemist at another institute. It fails in every attempt. A colleague says the original lab 'always had a trick' not written down. Her group wants to publish a negative-result note and move on; the original author is on the committee that will review her institute's funding. She must decide what to do.
options: Publish the failed replication with full methods and data, accepting any tension with the original author.
Email the original author for the missing details first and wait for a reply before publishing anything.
Drop the project quietly and quietly warn colleagues informally, avoiding the risk to funding but leaving the literature unchanged.

title: The honest mistake found after publication
scenario: Senior author Dr. Elin Sigurdsson in Reykjavik finds a coding error in her team's published analysis of fish stock decline: a sign flip changed one regional trend. The overall conclusion mostly holds, but a policy report has used the erroneous figure to justify a quota cut affecting small fishing towns. Retraction would harm her junior co-authors' early careers. She must decide how to correct the record.
options: Request a retraction and republish the corrected analysis, prioritising a clear record over reputational costs.
Issue a formal correction notice rather than a retraction, as the main conclusion stands.
Notify the policy agency directly first and let them decide whether to revisit the quota, then submit a correction.
tension: transparency vs. harm to junior colleagues

title: Ghost data in a thesis
scenario: Thesis examiner Professor Daniel Okonkwo-Reyes in Manila is reading a PhD thesis in which a table's numbers, he realises, match those in a student's earlier unpublished master's thesis from a different university, yet with different units. The candidate is a scholarship holder whose family has sacrificed much. The examination board meets tomorrow, and other examiners seem pleased. Daniel may have misread. He must decide how to act.
options: Raise the discrepancy with the board tomorrow and ask for the candidate's explanation before any decision.
Contact the candidate directly first to give a chance to clarify, then decide whether to raise it formally.
Pass the thesis with a note recommending further checks, avoiding an accusation without clear proof.
tension: fairness to the candidate vs. standards

title: Photoshopped micrographs on a deadline
scenario: Junior researcher Camila Torres in Bogotá is asked by her lab head to 'clean up' a microscopy image for a grant renewal by removing a smudge that overlaps a cell of interest. Cloning in neighbouring pixels would be quick. The head says everyone does it and it does not change the finding. The renewal deadline is tonight and the lab's four jobs depend on it. Camila has the original file. She must decide what to do.
options: Make the edit as asked, given it is cosmetic and the grant is crucial for the whole lab.
Refuse and submit the unedited image with a note about the smudge, even if it weakens the application.
Retake the image tomorrow and ask for a short extension, risking the deadline but avoiding manipulation.

title: A whistleblower's anonymous email
scenario: Research integrity officer Dr. Kirsten Aalto in Helsinki receives an anonymous email alleging that a rising star in the physics department plagiarised methods and invented a measurement set. The tip includes plausible details but no evidence, and it arrives days before a major prize committee decision. The accused has an unblemished record. Opening a formal inquiry would become known quickly. Kirsten must decide how to respond.
options: Open a confidential preliminary inquiry immediately, treating the specific allegations seriously regardless of anonymity.
Ask the anonymous sender for more evidence and do nothing formal until it arrives.
Open the inquiry but delay it until after the prize decision to avoid influencing the committee, a choice others may see as favouritism.
tension: presumption of innocence vs. due diligence

title: Selective reporting of side effects
scenario: Medical writer Hannah Lindqvist, freelancing from Gothenburg, is drafting a trial manuscript for a drugmaker. The sponsor's team asks her to describe a cluster of dizziness cases as 'unrelated to treatment' based on a post hoc review, although the investigators initially coded them as probably related. The sponsor is her biggest client. Her contract has a confidentiality clause. She must decide what to write.
options: Write what the sponsor requested, relying on its team's authority over interpretation.
Present both the original and the post hoc coding transparently in the text, even if the sponsor objects.
Decline the assignment and end the contract, leaving someone else to write the manuscript.

title: Salami-slicing a single study
scenario: Early-career lecturer Rashid Al-Mansoori in Muscat has one solid study on teacher burnout. His department's promotion system counts paper numbers, and colleagues routinely split one dataset into four papers. Splitting would mean overlapping text and partial redundancy. Promotion would raise his pay and let him support parents. A single long paper would also take a year to be reviewed, while shorter papers move faster through his regional journals. He must decide whether to publish as one paper or several.
options: Publish one comprehensive paper, accepting a slower promotion path but a cleaner record.
Split into several papers as colleagues do, citing each and being open about the shared dataset.
Publish one main paper and a distinct second paper using genuinely different analyses, a compromise that may still be questionable.
tension: personal need vs. norms of publication

title: Lost lab notebooks and a patent
scenario: University technology transfer officer Dr. Adaeze Nwosu in Cape Town is reviewing a patent claiming a new water-filter membrane. The inventor, a professor, says the original lab notebooks flooded in a storm. Some students recall that the key idea came from a former student who left the programme. The licensing deal with a local company would create jobs. Adaeze must decide how to proceed with filing.
options: File the patent naming only the professor, relying on the available evidence and protecting the deal.
Add the former student as inventor after trying to contact them, even if it complicates the deal.
Pause filing until the contributions are investigated through interviews, risking a missed priority date.

title: Imputed missing data and a funding round
scenario: Biostatistician Dr. Ji-woo Han in Seoul leads analysis of a hospital infection-control programme. Thirty percent of outcome data are missing, probably not at random. Her director wants to present a result using a generous imputation method that shows a strong benefit, ahead of a budget decision for ten hospitals. A more cautious method shows a smaller, uncertain effect. Both are statistically defensible. Ji-woo must choose what to present.
options: Present the generous imputation as the main result, with the method clearly stated, since it is a legitimate approach.
Present the cautious method as primary, accepting the risk that funding is cut.
Present both side by side with an explanation of the uncertainty, leaving decision-makers to weigh them.

title: Peer reviewer spots the editor's own conflict
scenario: Reviewer Dr. Ferdinand Bauer in Vienna is asked to assess a manuscript that heavily praises a software tool, then notices the handling editor co-founded the company selling it, which is not disclosed in the paper. The paper is otherwise sound. Journals in this field are small and Ferdinand relies on the editor for future invitations. The deadline for his review is tomorrow. He must decide what to write.
options: Flag the undisclosed link to the editor-in-chief in confidential comments, whatever the consequences.
Review the science only and ignore the link, since it is the editor's responsibility to manage conflicts.
Contact the editor privately to ask whether a conflict declaration is needed, giving a chance to fix it quietly.

title: Rat study results that vanish at replication
scenario: Neuroscientist Dr. Amara Diallo in Dakar finds that her own earlier published finding, on a stress hormone and memory in rats, did not replicate in a larger, preregistered follow-up. The original paper launched her career and appears in grant criteria she helped write. A colleague suggests framing the new work as 'refining boundary conditions.' Retracting the old paper is possible but not required. Amara must decide how to describe the new result.
options: Publish the failed replication plainly as contradicting the earlier paper, and consider asking for retraction.
Frame it as a boundary-condition refinement, which may be partly true but understates the contradiction.
Publish the replication and add a note to the original paper's journal, leaving retraction to the editors.

title: A grad student reuses a model's output
scenario: Supervisor Professor Eun-Kyung Shin in Busan discovers that her master's student used a large language model to write the results section of a thesis, including some sentences that describe analyses never run. The student is frightened, saying he was overwhelmed by a sick parent and weak English. Policy allows disclosed tool use but forbids fabrication. Graduation is next month. She must decide what to do.
options: Report to the integrity committee as policy requires, since fabricated analyses were described.
Require the student to rewrite honestly with a disclosure of tool use and handle the case informally.
Delay graduation by a semester and require supervised rewriting, balancing accountability and mercy.

title: The telescope time that was never used
scenario: Observatory staff scientist Dr. Alejandro Navarro in Santiago reviews a postdoc's paper on a distant galaxy. The logs show the telescope was not pointed at the target on the claimed night; data may have come from an archive of another team, without permission. The postdoc says he mislabelled dates. The paper is in press, and the collaboration includes seven institutions. Alejandro must decide how to proceed.
options: Alert the journal and the collaboration's leads immediately to pause publication pending clarification.
Ask the postdoc for the raw files and verify first, before involving anyone else.
Say nothing until the paper appears and then raise an erratum, avoiding disruption at a delicate stage.

title: Contradictory results from a donor-funded centre
scenario: Economist Dr. Folasade Adebayo-Clarke in Ibadan runs an evaluation of a microcredit programme whose donor also funds her centre. Her results show no improvement in household income and some increase in debt stress. The donor's programme officer has hinted that 'timing and framing' matter ahead of a replenishment meeting. The centre employs twenty people. She must decide how to report.
options: Publish the findings as they are, on the agreed timeline, even if the donor is displeased.
Delay publication by a few months until after the replenishment meeting to protect the centre's survival.
Share findings with the donor first and invite comment, retaining final editorial control but accepting pressure.

title: A mentor's suspicious dataset in a shared repository
scenario: Data curator Ingrid Solheim in Bergen manages a shared repository where a retired professor deposits datasets for ageing research. She notices his latest uploaded numbers have an unnatural digit distribution, a known sign of fabrication, though it could be a rounding artefact. The professor is beloved and in poor health. Hundreds of downstream users will rely on the data. Ingrid must decide whether to act.
options: Flag the dataset publicly with a quality warning pending clarification, to protect downstream users.
Contact the professor's former department privately and ask them to investigate before any public notice.
Do nothing, since she is a curator and not an investigator, and her statistical impression is not proof.

title: Paper mill offer to a struggling hospital physician
scenario: Clinician Dr. Nguyen Thi Lan in Hanoi must publish an indexed paper to keep her promotion eligibility. A broker offers authorship on a ready-made case series for 600 dollars, a third of her monthly salary. The data look plausible but she cannot verify the patients exist. Many colleagues have done the same. Her hospital is short-staffed and she has little research time. She must decide.
options: Decline and try to produce a small honest study, accepting delay or loss of promotion.
Buy the authorship, since the system's demands are unrealistic and the content seems harmless.
Offer to collaborate with the broker's source on a case series from her real patients, a grey path that may still be exploitative.

title: A retraction request from the author himself
scenario: Journal editor Dr. Mirjam Kessler in Zurich receives a letter from an author asking her to retract his own five-year-old paper because he now doubts the data collected by a former student. No independent check has been done. The paper has influenced clinical guidelines. The student, now abroad, denies any error. The author is close to retirement. Mirjam must decide whether to retract.
options: Retract promptly on the author's request, since he is best placed to know and guidelines may rest on it.
Open an independent investigation of the data before deciding, protecting the student from unproven blame.
Publish an expression of concern first, signalling doubt while the matter is examined.
tension: speed vs. fairness to a third party

title: Cherry-picked climate model runs
scenario: Modeller Dr. Tendai Moyo in Harare is asked by a consultancy to select a subset of climate simulations for a dam-feasibility report, and the subset the client prefers shows reliable rainfall. The full ensemble shows wide uncertainty and a real drought risk. The dam would bring electricity to a district that has none, and funders will drop the project if risks look high. Tendai is paid per deliverable. He must decide what to include.
options: Use the preferred subset as requested, documenting selection criteria, since the dam would help many people.
Present the full ensemble with its uncertainty, even if the dam loses funding.
Present the full ensemble and also propose design adjustments such as storage, hoping to keep the project alive.

title: A coauthor who wants to delete the raw data
scenario: Research assistant Takeshi Mori in Sapporo is told by his senior co-author to delete raw sensor files from a seabird tracking project to free server space after the paper appears. Funder rules require keeping data for ten years. The senior author says nobody ever checks and storage costs money the lab lacks. Takeshi notices that some tracks in the paper looked inconsistent with the raw files. He must decide what to do.
options: Delete the files as told, since it's the senior author's decision and storage is a real constraint.
Keep a private copy against instructions, preserving the evidence and the funder's rule.
Raise the retention rule and the inconsistency with the department head, bypassing the co-author at some risk.

title: A student's innocent overlap with a famous theory
scenario: Mathematics professor Dr. Zsofia Varga in Budapest receives a student's thesis that closely echoes an unpublished idea she mentioned in a seminar two years ago, though the student claims independent discovery and cites nothing. She is flattered but uneasy. The student is brilliant and poor and needs the degree to retain a stipend. Zsofia has no written record. She must decide how to handle the overlap.
options: Raise it with the student and request acknowledgement of her seminar, accepting the awkwardness.
Let it pass, accepting independent invention as plausible and the student's need as weightier.
Ask the student to explain the derivation in an oral discussion first, then decide, risking a charged encounter.

title: Rushed preprint with a shaky result
scenario: Epidemiologist Dr. Olumide Bakare in Abuja has an early analysis suggesting a widely used antimalarial reduces severity of a new viral illness. The sample is small and confounded. The ministry wants guidance within days, and competing groups may post first. Posting a preprint with caveats may trigger mass use of the drug and shortages for malaria patients. He must decide what to release.
options: Post the preprint with strong caveats now to inform decisions and claim priority.
Hold the finding until a larger, cleaner analysis is complete, accepting the risk that others publish first.
Share the preliminary data privately with the ministry's technical committee only, not publicly.
tension: public information vs. misuse of weak results
